If responses are coded as ‘2’, ‘7’, or ‘8’, the participant should skip to the end of the section. 2. Main Source of App Access: Participants are asked to identify their primary source of access to mobile applications. 3. Internet Usage: Participants are queried about their purposes for using the internet. If responses include ‘A’, ‘Y’, or ‘Z’, no other options can be selected. 4. Mobile App Usage: Participants are asked about their specific uses for mobile applications. If responses include ‘A’, ‘Y’, or ‘Z’, no other options can be selected. 5. Profiles on Dating or Hook-Up Platforms: Participants are asked whether they have profiles or accounts on any dating, sexual, or hook-up websites or applications. If responses are coded as ‘2’, ‘7’, or ‘8’, they should skip to the end of the current section. 6. Specific Sites or Apps with Profiles: Participants are asked to specify the sites or apps where they have created profiles. 7. HIV Knowledge and Perceptions: Understanding how HIV is transmitted is critical for promoting safer sexual behaviors and reducing stigma faced by individuals living with HIV. It is equally important to dispel misconceptions about HIV transmission, as these can hinder the adoption of safer practices and perpetuate stigma. 8. HIV Knowledge Questions: Can a healthy-looking person have HIV? Can HIV be transmitted through mosquito bites? 9. Game of Contacts (GoC): The Game of Contacts is a method used to estimate the social visibility of hard-to-reach populations, such as sex workers, transgender individuals, people who inject drugs, or men who have sex with men. This technique involves using a board and playing cards, each displaying a first name. Participants are asked how many people they know with a given name and provide information about these individuals. The game continues until a pre-determined number of cards have been played. The data collected helps estimate the social visibility of these populations, ranging from 0 (no visibility) to 1 (complete visibility). 10. Questionnaire Feedback and Interview Status: This module is primarily for the interviewer to document feedback, such as the time taken to complete the interview and whether the participant completed the survey. Negative feedback or high non-completion rates should be addressed promptly. Questions should be adapted to the local context. 11. Peer Recruitment in Respondent-Driven Sampling (RDS): This module measures non-response rates in RDS surveys by asking recruiters about the number of people they offered coupons to, how many refused, and the reasons for refusal. This data helps identify potential biases in response rates and differences between participants and non-participants. 12. Time-Location Sampling (TLS): Time-location sampling is used to access hard-to-reach populations at high risk for HIV by sampling locations where these populations gather. Questions in this module measure the frequency of attendance at specific venues and the number of different venues visited. These questions should be tailored to the local context and the population being surveyed. 13. Venue Attendance Frequency: Participants are asked how many times in the last 30 days they visited places where specific populations (e.g., gay men, people who inject drugs, or sex workers) socialize. Examples of such venues include bars, clubs, parks, social organizations, and other relevant locations.
